title: “YOU ARE GODS” — The Verse People Keep Using to Make Themselves Bigger… When Jesus Was Revealing Someone Greater
paragraphs: “YOU ARE GODS” — The Verse People Keep Using to Make Themselves Bigger… When Jesus Was Revealing Someone Greater

What Jesus Really Meant in John 10:34—and why one of the Bible’s most misunderstood statements was never permission to make yourself divine, but part of a breathtaking confrontation pointing us toward the unique Son of God.
There are four words in the Bible that can become dangerous when they are ripped away from the words surrounding them.
“You are gods.”
Jesus said them.
That is exactly why they can sound so convincing when someone isolates them.
Maybe you have heard someone quote John 10:34 as though Jesus finally revealed humanity’s hidden secret:
“You don’t know how powerful you are.”
“You have divinity inside you.”
“You are a little god.”
“You can create your own reality.”
“You just need to awaken to who you really are.”
And because the words appear in red letters in many Bibles, the argument can feel almost impossible to challenge.
After all…
Jesus said it.
But what if those four words were never meant to exalt you?
What if Jesus was quoting a judgment passage?
What if the original text actually destroys human pride instead of feeding it?
And what if the most astonishing truth in this passage is not that you are a god…
…but that the true Son of God came into a world full of people trying to take God's place—and still chose to save them?
Stay with the passage.
Because context changes everything.
Jesus is standing in Jerusalem during the Feast of Dedication.
The tension around Him has become unbearable.
His opponents surround Him and demand an answer.
If He is the Messiah, they want Him to say it plainly.
Jesus points them toward His works. He speaks about His sheep. He says that no one can snatch them from His hand. Then He says that no one can snatch them from His Father's hand.
And then comes the sentence that detonates the conversation:
“I and the Father are one.”
The Greek is striking:
ἐγὼ καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἕν ἐσμεν
Egō kai ho Patēr hen esmen.
“I and the Father are one.”
Notice something important.
Jesus does not say, “Everyone is God.”
He does not say, “You are one with God in exactly the same way I am.”
He speaks about Himself and the Father.
His opponents understand His words as an extraordinary claim, because they immediately pick up stones.
Jesus asks them why.
They answer that it is not because of His good works but because, in their accusation, He—a man—was making Himself God.
And that is where Jesus says the words so often pulled out of context:
“Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’?”
In Greek:
ἐγὼ εἶπα· θεοί ἐστε
Egō eipa: theoi este.
“I said, you are gods.”
But Jesus did not invent that sentence during this confrontation.
He was quoting Scripture.
Specifically, Psalm 82:6.
And once you go back to the psalm Jesus quoted, something fascinating happens.
The Hebrew reads:
אֲנִי־אָמַרְתִּי אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם
Ani amarti, elohim attem.
“I said, you are elohim.”
The word that immediately demands our attention is:
אֱלֹהִים — elohim.
Yes, elohim is the familiar Hebrew word frequently used for God.
But words receive their precise sense from context.
The mere appearance of elohim does not automatically mean that everyone described with the term possesses the unique, uncreated being of Yahweh.
And Psalm 82 certainly does not suddenly announce the existence of multiple Almighty Gods competing with the LORD.
Read what happens next.
The beings addressed as elohim are condemned.
They have failed in justice.
The weak have suffered.
The needy have been neglected.
The wicked have received favor.
And then comes the line that almost never appears on the motivational quote:
“Nevertheless, like man you shall die.”
That changes the atmosphere completely.
“You are gods” is followed by death and judgment.
Whatever precisely elohim identifies in Psalm 82, the passage is not a coronation ceremony teaching ordinary people to discover that they are independent deities.
It is a courtroom.
And God is Judge.
There is an important interpretive question here, and Christians should be honest enough not to pretend it does not exist.

For centuries, many interpreters have understood the elohim of Psalm 82 as human rulers or judges exercising delegated authority under God. Other scholars understand Psalm 82 against the ancient biblical picture of a heavenly or divine council and therefore identify these elohim as created spiritual beings under Yahweh's absolute authority.
The disagreement is real.
But notice what neither interpretation requires:
That every human being is an autonomous god possessing the same divine nature as the LORD.
That idea simply is not what Jesus is teaching here.
In fact, Jesus continues His argument immediately:

“If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”
Read that slowly.
Jesus does not quote Psalm 82 and then announce:
“See? Everybody is God.”
He draws attention back to Himself.
To the One whom the Father sanctified.
To the One whom the Father sent into the world.
To the Son.
His argument moves from the lesser case toward the greater.

If Scripture can employ such extraordinary terminology for beings subordinate to God without Scripture becoming guilty of blasphemy, His opponents cannot simply hear the title “Son of God,” scream “blasphemy,” and refuse to examine the identity, works, and mission of the One standing before them.
Jesus tells them, in effect, to examine His works.
And then John records another staggering statement:
“the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”
The center of the passage is still Christ.
That matters.
Because human beings have been reaching for God's throne since Eden.
The serpent's temptation was not merely about forbidden fruit.
It attacked trust in God.
“God is withholding something.”
“You could have more.”
“You could determine good and evil for yourself.”
“You could be like God.”
Humanity reached upward.
And fell.
That ancient temptation still knows how to dress itself for every generation.
Sometimes it wears religious clothing.
Sometimes spiritual clothing.
Sometimes self-help clothing.
Sometimes it sounds almost Christian.
“You have limitless power within yourself.”
“You create reality with your words.”
“You don't really need rescue; you need awakening.”
“You aren't a sinner needing reconciliation—you've simply forgotten your divinity.”
Then somebody discovers John 10:34.
“You are gods.”
Four words.
A whole theology built upon them.
But Jesus never came to awaken us to our supposed independent deity.
Jesus came to save sinners.
That distinction is enormous.
Christianity does proclaim something breathtaking about human beings.
We are created in God's image.
We may become children of God through faith in Christ.
Believers are united with Christ.
The Holy Spirit dwells in God's people.
Christians are being transformed into Christ's likeness.
Peter can even speak of believers becoming “partakers of the divine nature” in 2 Peter 1:4—a text that Christian theology has discussed deeply across the centuries.
But participation in God's life by grace is not the same thing as becoming God by nature.
The Creator remains Creator.
We remain creatures.
Redeemed creatures can be brought unimaginably close to God without becoming another Almighty God.
That is not an insult to humanity.
It is something far more beautiful.
You don't have to be God to be loved by God.
You don't have to possess omnipotence to matter.
You don't have to manufacture your own salvation.
You don't have to speak universes into existence.
You don't have to pretend you are limitless.
You are allowed to be a creature held by your Creator.
You are allowed to say:
“I need You.”
And perhaps that is where this passage becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us would rather discover secret power inside ourselves than admit desperate need before Jesus.
Power sounds attractive.
Repentance does not.
Self-deification strokes the ego.
The cross crucifies it.
“Discover the god within you” asks very little of your pride.
“Deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Me” asks for everything.
And yet the cross is where grace begins doing what pride could never accomplish.
Because the Gospel is not the story of humans finally realizing they were gods.
It is the story of the Son of God entering the ruin humans created by trying to live without God.
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered His creation.
The Holy One walked among sinners.
The innocent Christ was condemned.
The King wore thorns.
Hands that healed were pierced.
The One who deserved worship received mockery.
Jesus carried sin to the cross, died, was buried, and rose again.
Not because humanity needed a motivational speech about its hidden greatness.
Because humanity needed a Savior.
Maybe that is what makes grace so difficult for proud hearts to receive.
Grace requires you to admit that you cannot rescue yourself.
You cannot outgrow sin.
You cannot manifest away guilt.
You cannot rename rebellion enlightenment.
You cannot save yourself by discovering some hidden spark of deity.
You need forgiveness.
So do I.
We need Christ.
And the beautiful scandal of Christianity is that when sinners finally stop pretending to be their own gods, they discover that the true God is more merciful than they imagined.
Maybe you have been running.
Maybe nobody knows what is happening inside you.
Church people see the smile.
Family sees the version of you that you know how to perform.
Facebook sees the photographs.
Friends hear “I'm okay.”
But God sees the secret.
The addiction.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair nobody knows about.
The anger.
The envy.
The pride.
The private messages.
The compromises.
The prayerlessness.
The doubts you are afraid to say aloud.
The nights when you wonder whether you have wandered too far to come home.
And here is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Jesus did not come for a fictional, polished version of you.
Christ died for sinners.
The Gospel does not tell you to hide your scandal until you become worthy of grace.
Grace meets sinners in the scandal and calls them into repentance, forgiveness, holiness, and new life.
That does not make sin small.
The cross proves sin is more serious than we want to believe.
But the same cross proves something else.
God's grace in Christ reaches deeper than the grave.
This is why Jesus must remain at the center of John 10.
Not us.
Not our supposed divinity.
Jesus.
The Son whom the Father sent.
The Shepherd whose sheep hear His voice.
The One who gives eternal life.
The One whose works bear witness to Him.
The One who is in the Father and the Father in Him.
The One standing before people holding stones…
while knowing He would soon surrender Himself to nails.
And perhaps the question John 10 ultimately presses into your heart is not:
“Am I a god?”
Perhaps the real question is:
What will I do with the Son of God?
You can study the Greek and still avoid Him.
You can debate elohim and never surrender.
You can win an argument about Psalm 82 while losing sight of the Shepherd calling you.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
But the Scriptures were never given merely so that we could become cleverer sinners.
They lead us toward truth.
And truth brings us face-to-face with Jesus Christ.
So if you have used “you are gods” to build yourself a throne, come down.
If someone taught you that Christianity is ultimately about discovering that you possess God's unique deity, come back to the text.
If pride has convinced you that you don't need repentance, come back to the cross.
And if shame has convinced you that Jesus would never receive someone like you…
come back to the cross too.
Pride says, “I don't need saving.”
Shame says, “I can't be saved.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Jesus says to repent and believe the good news.
The answer to your sin is not pretending you are divine.
The answer is the crucified and risen Christ.
Don't turn the comments into a place for theological performance.
Let them become a place where somebody realizes they are not the only person fighting to come home.
And think of one person who needs this article.
Not twenty random names.
One.

Maybe a friend has encountered teaching about “little gods.” Maybe someone you love is being pulled toward spirituality that borrows Christian vocabulary while quietly removing Christ from the center. Maybe someone believes his scandal has already written the final chapter of his life.
Stay because you want more Scripture.
Stay because you want your theology tested against the Word instead of whatever happens to be trending.
Stay because following Jesus is worth taking seriously.
Read them.
Save them.
Study them.
Share them.
Send them to the struggling believer.
Send them to the seeker.
Send them to the lukewarm Christian.
Even send them to the unbelieving friend willing to investigate who Jesus really is.
remember Jesus.
Scripture does not need us to make ourselves bigger.
It reveals a Christ greater than we imagined.
And maybe tonight the most freeing prayer you could pray is not:
“God, show me how powerful I am.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, show me who You are. Show me who I really am before You. Forgive what must be forgiven. Break what must be broken. Heal what must be healed. And teach me to follow You.”
Because the greatest miracle in this passage was never that sinful humanity could steal God's title.
It is that the true Son of God would come looking for sinners anyway.
Your scandal does not have to write your final sentence.
Put down the crown you were never meant to carry—and receive the grace only the King could give.
